hero.title: Engine Warranty Guide what you need to know before you buy
hero.description: Warranties vary by supplier. Understanding the differences saves you stress later.

ordered.title: What this guide covers
ordered.description: When you buy a replacement engine through Engines Market, the warranty comes from the supplier - not from us. We do not provide, administer, or enforce warranties. But we can help you understand what to look for, what questions to ask, and how to avoid common pitfalls.

items: The different types of warranty
What is typically covered (and what is not)
How long warranties usually last
Questions you should ask every supplier
What to do if something goes wrong

ordered.title: Parts-only vs Parts and Labour
ordered.description: Most engine suppliers offer two main types of warranty. The difference is significant.

rows: The replacement engine itself (if it fails due to manufacturing defect)
Labour to remove and refit the engine; diagnosis; fluids; gaskets; consequential damage
The replacement engine plus the labour cost to remove the faulty unit and refit the replacement
Consequential damage (e.g., damage to other components caused by engine failure); towing; rental car

blocks.text: Key question to ask: “If the engine fails within the warranty period, who pays for the labour to swap it out again-”
If the answer is anything other than “the supplier covers labour as well”, you have a parts-only warranty.
Most engine warranties (especially on reconditioned and rebuilt units) cover:

items: Internal lubricated parts - crankshaft, connecting rods, pistons, piston rings, camshafts, valves, valve springs, rocker arms, lifters, oil pump
Timing components - timing chain, belt, tensioners, guides (if they fail due to manufacturing defect)
Gaskets and seals - but only if they fail as a direct result of another covered component failing (not as standalone items)

blocks.text: Important: Coverage always depends on the supplier’s exact warranty terms. Always read the written document - not just what you are told over the phone.
Almost no engine warranty covers everything. These exclusions are standard across the industry:

rows: Considered wear items. Head gaskets, valve cover gaskets, sump gaskets, crank seals, cam seals - these are almost never covered as standalone failures.
Parts-only warranties specifically exclude labour. Even some parts-and-labour warranties may limit the labour rate (e.g., £60 per hour, not the garage’s actual rate).
If the engine fails and damages the turbo, DPF, catalytic converter, or radiator - those parts are not covered. Only the engine itself.
If the engine was fitted incorrectly (wrong oil, wrong torque settings, damaged sensors), the warranty is void.
Running without oil, ignoring warning lights, overheating, racing, towing beyond capacity - all void warranties.
Remapping, tuning, performance upgrades - most suppliers exclude these immediately.
Oil, coolant, filters, drive belts - not covered even if the engine is replaced under warranty.
Transport costs to return a failed engine or to receive a replacement are rarely covered.
The cost to diagnose the failure is usually not covered - only the repair or replacement itself.

blocks.text: Ask before you buy: “Can you send me a written copy of your full warranty exclusions-”
If a supplier hesitates or says “it’s standard”, that is a red flag.

ordered.title: Warranty duration - what to expect by engine condition
ordered.description: Longer warranties generally mean the supplier has more confidence in their product. But duration alone is not everything - you also need to check what is covered.

rows: Parts and labour (check the labour cap)
Rebuilt engine (your own engine sent away)
Parts and labour (higher confidence from the rebuilder)

blocks.text: Note: These are typical ranges based on the UK market. Your supplier’s actual terms may differ. Always confirm in writing.

ordered.title: Questions you must ask every supplier
ordered.description: Copy these questions and ask every supplier before you agree to anything.

items: “What exactly does your warranty cover - parts only, or parts and labour-”
“How long does the warranty last - from the date of invoice-”
“Is there a mileage limit (e.g., 12,000 miles per year)-”
“What is excluded from your warranty- Please send me a written list.”
“If the engine fails, who pays for the labour to remove and refit it-”
“Is there a cap on the labour rate you will cover (e.g., £60 per hour)-”
“What happens if the engine fails and damages other components - are those covered-”
“Do I have to use your preferred garage for the refit, or can I choose my own-”
“What records do I need to keep (service history, oil change receipts)-”
“Who do I contact if I need to make a claim - and what is their response time-”
Keep the invoice and warranty document somewhere safe.
Note the date the warranty starts and ends.
Follow the supplier’s maintenance recommendations (e.g., oil change intervals, oil grade).
Keep receipts for any servicing or repairs done during the warranty period.

ordered.title: The warranty claim process - what to expect
ordered.description: If your replacement engine develops a problem within the warranty period, here is the typical journey.

cards.title: Stop driving immediately
cards.text: If you hear knocking, rattling, loss of power, or see warning lights - stop driving to prevent further damage. Driving a failing engine usually voids the warranty.
cards.fullText: 1 Stop driving immediately If you hear knocking, rattling, loss of power, or see warning lights - stop driving to prevent further damage. Driving a failing engine usually voids the warranty.

cards.title: Contact the supplier first
cards.text: Call or email the supplier who sold you the engine. Explain the symptoms. Do not take the car to another garage without telling the supplier first - they may need to inspect the engine themselves.
cards.fullText: 2 Contact the supplier first Call or email the supplier who sold you the engine. Explain the symptoms. Do not take the car to another garage without telling the supplier first - they may need to inspect the engine themselves.

cards.title: Provide documentation
cards.text: The supplier will ask for: the original invoice, warranty document, photos or videos of the issue (if visible), fault codes (if available), and service records (oil changes, etc.).
cards.fullText: 3 Provide documentation The supplier will ask for: the original invoice, warranty document, photos or videos of the issue (if visible), fault codes (if available), and service records (oil changes, etc.).

cards.title: Supplier diagnoses the fault
cards.text: They may ask you to bring the vehicle to them, or to an approved garage, for inspection. They will determine if the failure is covered by the warranty.
cards.fullText: 4 Supplier diagnoses the fault They may ask you to bring the vehicle to them, or to an approved garage, for inspection. They will determine if the failure is covered by the warranty.

cards.title: Claim approved or declined
cards.text: Approved: The supplier will arrange a replacement engine and (if parts-and-labour) cover the refit labour. You may need to pay for consumables (oil, coolant, gaskets). Declined: The supplier will explain why (e.g., installation error, neglect, excluded part). You can appeal if you disagree.
cards.fullText: 5 Claim approved or declined Approved: The supplier will arrange a replacement engine and (if parts-and-labour) cover the refit labour. You may need to pay for consumables (oil, coolant, gaskets). Declined: The supplier will explain why (e.g., installation error, neglect, excluded part). You can appeal if you disagree.

cards.title: Escalate if necessary
cards.text: If the supplier refuses a valid claim or becomes unresponsive, you may have legal rights under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. For disputes about the supplier’s warranty, Engines Market does not mediate - but we do track complaints as part of our supplier monitoring. For a more detailed walkthrough, see our Warranty claims guide .
cards.fullText: 6 Escalate if necessary If the supplier refuses a valid claim or becomes unresponsive, you may have legal rights under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. For disputes about the supplier’s warranty, Engines Market does not mediate - but we do track complaints as part of our supplier monitoring. For a more detailed walkthrough, see our Warranty claims guide .

items: Get the warranty terms in writing before you pay
Ask about exclusions - especially gaskets and consequential damage
Keep all invoices and service receipts
Follow the supplier’s maintenance schedule
Contact the supplier first if something goes wrong
Assume a “12-month warranty” includes labour - ask
Ignore warning lights or unusual noises - that may void your cover
Use the wrong oil grade - it will void almost any warranty
Modify or remap the engine - that will also void cover
Drive a failing engine - you will make it worse and lose your claim

ordered.title: How Engines Market helps - even though we do not provide warranties
ordered.description: We are a comparison platform, not a warranty provider. But we help you in three ways:

items: Education - This guide and our warranty claims guide help you understand what to expect.

Vetted suppliers - Every supplier in our network has passed our 4-point check , including a sustained 4.0+ star average review. Poor warranty handling would affect their reviews and their place in our network.
Monitoring - We track complaints. If a supplier consistently fails to honour warranties, they are removed.

blocks.text: You still need to do your own due diligence. But we have removed the highest-risk suppliers from the equation.

cards.text: Does Engines Market provide warranties on engines- No. Never. The warranty comes from the supplier you choose. We do not sell, fit, or warranty engines.
cards.fullText: Does Engines Market provide warranties on engines- No. Never. The warranty comes from the supplier you choose. We do not sell, fit, or warranty engines.

cards.text: What is the most common reason a warranty claim is rejected- Installation error (wrong oil, incorrect torque, damaged sensors) and neglect (ignoring warning lights, overheating) are the top two reasons. Consequential damage (e.g., the failed engine damaging the turbo) is also frequently excluded.

If the supplier ceases trading, you may have no recourse. This is one reason we monitor supplier status and only accept established businesses (1+ year trading minimum).
